newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Morgan to brief NZ First on Maori TV saga.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Morgan to brief NZ First on Maori TV saga.

text.p: New Zealand First MP Tukoroirangi Morgan will give a full briefing to next week's caucus on the Aotearoa Television controversy, Deputy Prime Minister and NZ First leader Winston Peters said on Tuesday.
"Mr Morgan will be giving the caucus a full briefing next week when all the information that's required is in," Peters told journalists after a caucus meeting on Tuesday.

Morgan, a former director of Aotearoa Television, and director Morehu McDonald spent thousands of dollars on clothes at an up-market Auckland shop at Aotearoa's expense just weeks before Morgan was elected to parliament.
Morgan has said he had the authority to spend the money as part of his clothing allowance as an on-air presenter, but executives at the station have denied this.

On Monday cabinet withdrew approval for $4 million in funding for the Maori language station citing verbal reports from Commerce Ministry officials of "serious resrevations about the financial management and controls in place" at the station.
After the caucus Peters again stopped short of unequivocally backing Morgan.
"I have, how shall I put it, the confidence of his electorate that voted for him to be the member of parliament and it is their vote that matters not what you think or what critics think.
"In my case I have always understood that the MP serves the electorate and whilst he has the confidence of that electorate he has every entitlement to be in this parliament."

Asked if Morgan was still likely to be the chair of the Maori Affairs select committee, Peters said: "New Zealand First will be announcing spokespersonships and the Prime Minister will be announcing select committee chairpersonships very shortly," Peters said.

Parliament's rules, known as standing orders, direct that the committees elect their own chairpersons. But with committees normally comprising eight members the votes could be split four- four between the government and opposition parties given the government's two seat majority in the House.
